opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olivia, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I manage a clothing store for a chain. A good team, smaller than it used to be. I'm the one between them and head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it helps with rotas and emails. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, head office will keep cutting hours whether AI does anything or not. That's the pressure I already live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Fight for my staff's hours, use the tools to save time on admin so I'm on the floor more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the way I always am at budget time.

S0.say: It helps with rotas and emails. Nothing dramatic.
S0.think: Head office will keep cutting hours anyway. That pressure's already there.
S0.do: Fights for her staff's hours and uses the tools to cut admin so she's on the floor more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To my team I'd say we're fine, stores need people. To head office I'd say give me the tools and I'll hit the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow still means my headcount keeps dropping. And no more Saturday kids learning the job. That's how I started, folding jumpers at seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train my best assistant manager on everything I know so she's ready. And I'd learn the new scheduling and stock tools properly so I'm useful to the area manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A slow squeeze, not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell your team they're fine. Do you believe it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, mostly. I wouldn't tell them about the targets I get each quarter, though. That's my worry to carry.

S1.say: Stores need people, so we're fine. And to head office: give me the tools and I'll hit the numbers.
S1.think: My headcount keeps dropping and there's no room left for teenagers to learn the job, like I did.
S1.do: Trains her best assistant manager and learns the new scheduling and stock tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say retail's always changed and we'll change with it. That's the company line, and I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think head office would use AI to do half of what I do, like rotas, stock orders and reports, and then merge my store with the one across town under one manager. That's a store manager gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the manager who gets the best results from the new systems, so if they merge, it's me who stays. I'd also update my CV and talk to my husband about our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel it getting closer.

S2.say: Retail has always changed and we'll change with it.
S2.think: Head office could hand half my job to AI, merge my store with the one across town and cut a manager.
S2.do: Aims to get the best results from the new systems so she's kept in a merger, updates her CV and reviews the budget with her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say we're focusing on customer experience, which is what head office would want me to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? Our customers are office workers. If they lose their jobs, they stop buying work clothes. Sales drop, stores close. And the managing part of my job is exactly what AI is good at. I'd be in trouble twice over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking outside retail, maybe managing in a hospital or a care setting, where it's people and physical work. I'd cut spending now, before anything happens, and stop putting money toward a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical work is safe in this picture, and your floor staff do physical work. Why would you be in trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they don't need me to manage them if a system sets the rota and the targets. The folding stays. The manager goes.

S3.think: My customers are office workers, and the managing part of my job is what AI is good at. I'd be in trouble twice over.
S3.do: Looks at management jobs in hospitals or care settings, cuts spending now and drops holiday savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after the people who've given their working lives to these stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the end of the store as I know it. Robots restocking at night, AI managing, self-checkout. My staff would go before me, and then me. And the care homes I'd thought of moving to get robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight to get my team decent payouts and references. I'd apply anywhere with people in it: schools, councils, anything. And we'd sit down as a family about what we can do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and sad. Mostly for my staff.

S4.say: We need to look after the people who've given their working lives to these stores.
S4.think: It's the end of the store as I know it. My staff go first, then me, and the care homes I'd thought of get robots too.
S4.do: Fights for decent payouts and references for her team, applies to schools and councils, and sits down with the family on what to cut.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sad, mostly for the staff.
